steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a robotics vision paper about benchmarking camera auto-exposure algorithms offline. Explain why HDR outdoor scenes are a problem for visual odometry, why comparing auto-exposure methods online is so hard, and present our emulation-based approach and dataset, ending with a list of contributions.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Cameras can capture the details of a scene at high resolution and high frame rates, and they are cost-effective. That is why they are used in many robotic applications, from object detection to localization. One of these applications is VO, which is the task of predicting how a camera moves between consecutive images. VO is the basis of many vision-based localization algorithms such as VSLAM, and improving it is still an active field of research. In outdoor settings, quick changes in the illumination level and HDR scenes can seriously compromise the performance of VO algorithms. A car leaving a tunnel can see an illumination variation over 120\text{\,}\mathrm{dB} in one second, but a standard 12-bit channel camera has a theoretical dynamic range of around 72\text{\,}\mathrm{dB}. Another example of such HDR environments is a boreal forest in winter, where the sun reflected on the snow has a strong contrast with the darkness of the trees. This contrast always leads to saturated pixels on both ends of the spectrum, which are shown with blue and red colorized hues in Figure 1, and so valuable information is lost for VO algorithms.

Because of this, researchers developed AE approaches that change the camera's parameters, like exposure time and gain, during operation, to reduce the impact of the dynamic range of the scene on VO.

  - common: one camera per method -> setup complex and expensive as methods grow
  - or: repeat identical trajectories per AE -> impractical for long trajectories
  - uncontrolled environment (Figure 1): illumination changes constantly -> no replicable benchmark
- Our proposal
  - equitable comparison of AE for robot localization; bracketing technique (cite) + realistic image emulation
  - \Delta t_{e} in Figure 1: generate images at any exposure time for recorded trajectories
  - multi-exposure dataset BorealHDR; multi-seasonal; Québec's forests and Laval University's Campus
  - 55 trajectories, more than 5 \mathrm{h} of recordings over 10 \mathrm{km}; 3D lidar scans, inertial measurements, GNSS

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Cameras can capture the details of a scene at high resolution and high frame rates, and they are cost-effective. That is why they are used in many robotic applications, from object detection to localization. One of these applications is VO, which is the task of predicting how a camera moves between consecutive images. VO is the basis of many vision-based localization algorithms such as VSLAM, and improving it is still an active field of research. In outdoor settings, quick changes in the illumination level and HDR scenes can seriously compromise the performance of VO algorithms. A car leaving a tunnel can see an illumination variation over 120\text{\,}\mathrm{dB} in one second, but a standard 12-bit channel camera has a theoretical dynamic range of around 72\text{\,}\mathrm{dB}. Another example of such HDR environments is a boreal forest in winter, where the sun reflected on the snow has a strong contrast with the darkness of the trees. This contrast always leads to saturated pixels on both ends of the spectrum, which are shown with blue and red colorized hues in Figure 1, and so valuable information is lost for VO algorithms.

Because of this, researchers developed AE approaches that change the camera's parameters, like exposure time and gain, during operation, to reduce the impact of the dynamic range of the scene on VO.

The problem is that exposure control is online, so comparing the methods is very challenging, because the test conditions have to be replicated exactly for each run, including the lighting of the environment and the camera poses. One common way to compare AE algorithms is to capture images with as many cameras as there are methods to benchmark. But when more methods are tested, the experimental setup gets more and more complex and expensive to manage. Another way is to replicate the same trajectories several times, once for each AE being evaluated, which is not practical for long trajectories. Also, in an uncontrolled environment like the one in Figure 1, the illumination changes all the time, so a replicable benchmark is impossible.

In this work we propose a new method for comparing AE algorithms for robot localization in an equitable way, based on the bracketing technique and realistic image emulation. As shown by \Delta t_{e} in Figure 1, our emulator framework can generate images at any exposure time we want for recorded trajectories. This is possible because of our multi-exposure dataset called BorealHDR, which we recorded in multi-seasonal conditions in Québec's forests and on Laval University's Campus. It has 55 trajectories, with more than 5 \mathrm{h} of recordings over 10 \mathrm{km}. It also has 3D lidar scans, inertial measurements and GNSS data. Because our dataset and emulation technique are new, we can benchmark AE algorithms, feature extraction and VO pipelines offline, which is not possible with single-exposure datasets. Our contributions are:

- 1. A new way to compare AE algorithms using an emulation framework that can generate realistic images at any plausible exposure time;

- 2. A multimodal dataset with stereo images at multiple exposures and 3D map references, in kilometer-scale HDR environments; and

- 3. The first offline benchmarking of seven AE algorithms on VO-based experiments.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Cameras can capture high-resolution details of a scene at high frame rates and in a cost-effective manner. For this reason, they are used in many robotic applications, ranging from object detection to localization. One such application is VO, the task of predicting the displacement of a camera between consecutive images. It is the basis of many vision-based localization algorithms, such as VSLAM, and improving it is still an active field of research [1,2]. In outdoor settings, quick variations in illumination level and HDR scenes can severely compromise the performance of VO algorithms [3]. In one second, a car leaving a tunnel can experience an illumination variation over 120\text{\,}\mathrm{dB} [4], while a standard 12-bit channel camera has a theoretical dynamic range of around 72\text{\,}\mathrm{dB}. A boreal forest in winter is another example of such an HDR environment, where the sun reflected on the snow strongly contrasts with the darkness of the trees. This contrast inevitably leads to saturated pixels on both ends of the spectrum, as highlighted by the blue and red colorized hues in Figure 1, resulting in a loss of valuable information for VO algorithms.

Accordingly, researchers have developed AE approaches that modify the camera's parameters, such as exposure time and gain, during operation in order to reduce the impact of the scene's dynamic range on VO [5,6,7].

Unfortunately, given the online nature of exposure control, comparing these methods is very challenging [8,9], as the test conditions, including environment lighting and camera poses, must be replicated exactly for each run. A frequent way of comparing AE algorithms is to capture images with as many cameras as there are methods to benchmark. As the number of tested methods grows, the experimental setup becomes increasingly complex and expensive to manage. Another alternative is to replicate identical trajectories multiple times, once for each evaluated AE, which is impractical for lengthy trajectories. Moreover, in an uncontrolled environment such as the one in Figure 1, the illumination changes constantly, making a replicable benchmark impossible.

In this work, we propose a novel method for an equitable comparison of AE algorithms applied to robot localization, based on the bracketing technique [10] and realistic image emulation. As illustrated by \Delta t_{e} in Figure 1, our emulator framework can generate images at any desired exposure time for recorded trajectories. This is made possible by our multi-exposure dataset, BorealHDR, recorded in multi-seasonal conditions in Québec's forests and on Laval University's Campus. It is composed of 55 trajectories, totaling more than 5 \mathrm{h} of recordings over 10 \mathrm{km}, and also includes 3D lidar scans, inertial measurements, and GNSS data. The novelty of our dataset and emulation technique allows us to benchmark AE algorithms, feature extraction and VO pipelines offline, as opposed to single-exposure datasets. In short, our contributions are the following:

- 1. A new comparison method for AE algorithms based on an emulation framework that can generate realistic images at any plausible exposure time;

- 2. A multimodal dataset providing stereo images at multiple exposures, alongside 3D map references, in kilometer-scale HDR environments; and

- 3. The first offline benchmarking of seven AE algorithms on VO-based experiments.
